opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the short version is that when you bundle everything into one monolithic loop, you can't reason about any single piece of it. When an agent fails, you don't know whether the model made a bad decision, the orchestration fed it the wrong context, or the execution environment did something unexpected. Splitting it into three layers gives you clean seams to debug, measure, and swap things out.

The way I think about it, there's the part that decides, which is the model and its reasoning. There's the part that coordinates, which handles state, memory, what context gets assembled, and how tasks get sequenced. And there's the part that acts, which is the actual interface to tools, sandboxes, and the outside world. Those three things change at very different rates. Models get better every few months. Your orchestration logic evolves with your product. Your execution layer is tied to infrastructure and security constraints that are much stickier. If they're tangled together, every model upgrade turns into a rewrite.

There's also a systems argument, which comes from my networking background. The internet works because of layering. You can innovate at one layer without everyone else agreeing to change. I think agents need the same property. If the execution layer has a well-defined contract, you can enforce permissions and isolation there, independent of whatever the model is doing. That's a much stronger safety story than hoping the prompt keeps the model in line.

And practically, it makes evaluation tractable. You can replay the execution layer deterministically, hold orchestration fixed, and compare models apples to apples. Or hold the model fixed and iterate on how you manage context. Without that separation, you're always changing three variables at once and calling it progress.

r005.rationale: It mentions permissions and isolation, but does not attribute secret-leakage protection to keeping secrets unexposed to the language model.

r006.rationale: It gives no account of sandbox snapshots or rolling back changes made during execution.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: So the honest answer is that it came out of pain, not out of some elegant theory. When we started building agents, everything was mashed together — the model call, the tool execution, the memory, the retry logic, the orchestration — all in one big loop. And that works great for a demo. It falls apart the moment you want to change anything.

So Exo splits it into three layers, and I think of them as answering three different questions. The bottom layer is: what can this thing actually do? That's tools, environment, the primitives the agent can touch — file systems, APIs, a browser, whatever. It's deterministic, it's testable, you can write unit tests against it like normal software. No model in there at all.

The middle layer is: how does the agent think? That's the model interface, the prompt construction, the context management, how you turn a goal and a history into the next action. This is the part that changes every three months because the models change every three months. If you've got this tangled up with your tools, every model upgrade becomes a rewrite.

And the top layer is: what's the policy? When do you stop, when do you ask a human, how many retries, what's the budget, what gets logged. That's the stuff that's really about the business or the product, not about the AI at all. And it's the stuff you want ops people and product people to be able to reason about without reading model prompts.

The reason I favor the decomposition is that those three things have completely different rates of change and completely different people who care about them. Tools are stable and owned by whoever owns the system you're wrapping. The reasoning layer churns with the frontier. The policy layer is a product decision. When you keep them separate, you can swap a model without touching your tools, you can tighten a safety policy without re-prompting anything, and crucially, when something goes wrong, you can actually tell which layer it went wrong in. That last one is underrated. Debugging a monolithic agent is miserable because you can't tell if the model was dumb, the tool was broken, or your loop had a bug. With the layers separated, the blast radius of any one change gets a lot smaller.

astra-6.text:
I favor that separation because those layers change for different reasons. You want to improve how an agent reasons without having to rewrite how it interacts with the world, and you want to change the underlying infrastructure without changing the agent’s behavior.

It also makes failures easier to understand. Did the agent make a bad decision, did the action fail, or did the system fail to provide the right context? If everything is bundled together, those look like the same problem: “the agent didn’t work.” Separate boundaries let you test and improve each part independently. That’s the main benefit for me—making the system easier to reason about as it gets more capable.

If an agent does the wrong thing, you want to understand where the failure happened, rather than treating the whole system as one opaque loop. You can test each layer, improve it, and swap implementations without rewriting everything else. The boundaries add some complexity, but they make the overall system easier to debug and evolve.
